text: Miriam Kastner, born on January 22, 1935, is a Bratislavan-born (former Czechoslovakia) Israeli-raised American oceanographer and geochemist. She is currently a distinguished professor at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego, where she has worked since 1972 and continues to serve in various leadership roles, including chair and vice chair of the faculty, associate director and director in the geosciences research division, chair of the Academic Senate Committee on Research, and curricular group coordinator of geological sciences. Kastner is recognized for her fundamental contributions to science and is well-regarded by colleagues. From an early age, she was drawn to the sciences and initially intended to become a mathematician, but later concluded that there were few career opportunities in mathematics, prompting her to explore other scientific fields due to the underrepresentation of women in science. She earned a minor in chemistry and a master's degree in geology from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in 1964, followed by a doctorate in geoscience from Harvard University in 1970. During her time at Harvard, she was the only woman in her department for three years, which created a discouraging environment where faculty members did not take women seriously and expected less of them, though some, including her Ph.D. committee, supported her. Kastner became the second female professor at Scripps Institution of Oceanography, joining just two months after the first geophysicist, thereby paving the way for future female scientists. Prior to joining Scripps, she worked as a research associate at Harvard until 1970 and then at the University of Chicago in 1971. Over her career, she has authored 174 articles and journals, with over 80 scientific articles specifically on fluid–rock interactions, primarily involving seawater. Her research focuses on mineralogy and petrology, with a central emphasis on fluid flow at subducting plate boundaries. She demonstrated that subsea hydrothermal vents were not known until the 1980s and explained that the ocean's volume circulates through hydrothermal systems once every five million years and through global subduction zones once every 200 million years, linking seafloor processes to Earth's long-term evolution. Her early work included a 1965 publication on glauconite, in which she identified flaws in prior studies due to neglect of non-structural iron oxides; she also studied diagenetic transformations of opal-A to opal-CT and quartz, dolomite formation controlled by pore-fluid geochemistry, and Sr distribution coefficients in calcite, which are critical for paleoclimate studies and indicating carbonate recrystallization. She revised the stability of P-O bonds in apatite and phosphate ions, leading to a recalculation of ocean phosphorus residence time. Her work on gas hydrates has contributed to understanding global warming and potential energy sources, helping to improve predictions of climate change and responses to anthropogenic perturbations. In the early 1990s, she conducted an experiment challenging a theory about dolomite leaching used in a forgery claim of the Getty kouros statue, a result later confirmed by Stanley Margolis. She has also compiled a synopsis of her 50 years of ocean drilling work, highlighting major projects such as the Mohole Project, Joides and Deep Sea Drilling Project, Ocean Drilling Program, and Integrated Ocean Drilling Program and International Ocean Discovery Program, each of which made significant contributions to geology. Kastner has served on the National Research Council's Ocean Studies Board from 2003 to 2005. As a woman in a male-dominated field, she noted difficulties in gaining support from science funding agencies, though she observed improvement in the number of women pursuing science degrees, even though only about 20% of women in science programs are field researchers. She encourages young women to have greater confidence in applying for field research positions, noting that support for women in the sciences has improved significantly compared to her earlier years.
